object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier from whom the organization can procure goods or services. Vendors are uniquely identified by a vendor number and are subject to status tracking and risk assessment.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
Every vendor has exactly one, and no two vendors share one... It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier assigned to each vendor upon creation in the supplier master.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official legal name of the vendor entity.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really...

object_types.name: TaxId
object_types.definition: The tax identification number of the vendor. Not unique due to parent-subsidiary structures and historical duplicates.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really...
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The operational status of a vendor: draft, active, or suspended.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.
Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on procurement spend level, set by the procurement team.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on compliance risk level, determined during the risk review process.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

object_types.name: Address
object_types.definition: A physical address associated with a vendor. Vendors may have multiple addresses for different purposes (remit-to, ship-from, legal).

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A compliance assessment record for a vendor, documenting risk evaluation, sign-off, and audit trail information. Multiple reviews can exist for a single vendor over time, with at most one marked as current.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.
Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review. Not zero, and the one has to be signed off.

object_types.name: ReviewId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Region
object_types.definition: A geographic region in which vendors may operate and maintain regional contacts. Currently four fixed regions: EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.
Four regions, fixed?... Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

object_types.name: RegionCode
object_types.definition: The code identifying a geographic region.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: Contact
object_types.definition: A primary contact person for a vendor within a specific region. Each vendor-region combination has exactly one primary contact.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.
Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region.
A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact. You cannot have two people both flagged primary for the same vendor in the same region -- the system rejects the second one.

ambiguities.description: Address granularity: The transcript mentions that vendors have 'three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one.' It is unclear whether these are three separate fields on the vendor record or whether the 'Address' value type is a single freetext field that contains undifferentiated multiple addresses. The model currently treats Address as a generic multi-valued attribute. To be precise, the model should either: (1) distinguish three separate address types (RemitToAddress, ShipFromAddress, LegalAddress) as separate value types, each with its own fact type, or (2) introduce an AddressType to create a ternary fact 'Vendor has Address of AddressType.' Without clarification, the semantics of the Address attribute are ambiguous.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Risk tier optionality and lifecycle: The transcript states 'A vendor with no review has no risk tier' (line 291) and 'Draft vendors don't have one' (line 287), but it does not explicitly clarify whether a Vendor in Draft status can NEVER have a RiskTier (logically impossible), or whether having a RiskTier implies the Vendor must be Active. The model interprets this as a subset constraint (if RiskTier exists, then RiskReview must exist), but the reverse direction is not addressed: can an Active vendor exist without a RiskTier? Clarify whether RiskTier is mandatory for Active vendors.

source_references.excerpt: Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier. Draft vendors don't have one... Every _active_ vendor has a current signed-off review. A draft vendor has no review at all -- that's the normal case, that's what draft means.

ambiguities.description: Current risk review identification: The transcript describes a Vendor accumulating multiple RiskReview records over its lifecycle, with 'at most one' marked as current. The model currently treats RiskReview as a separate entity type linked to Vendor by a 1-to-many fact type. However, there is no attribute or field specified to distinguish which review is 'current.' The model should clarify: (1) Is there a Boolean 'is_current' flag on each review? (2) Is 'current' derived from a latest-date calculation? (3) How does the system enforce the constraint that at most one review is current per vendor?

source_references.excerpt: But one of them is the current signed-off one... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one.

ambiguities.description: Vendor contact optionality per region: The transcript states 'If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all' (line 167), which suggests that the relationship 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact' is optional for vendors that do not operate in a region. However, it does not clarify the mandatory status for vendors that DO operate in a region: is the Contact mandatory once a Vendor-Region pair is established? The model assumes it is (based on line 163), but explicit confirmation is needed.

source_references.excerpt: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only.

ambiguities.description: Purchase order lifecycle and suspended vendor rule: The transcript explicitly parks a key business rule: 'what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided' (lines 279, 315). The participants debated whether suspension halts all orders, allows run-off, or requires a new 'run-off' status, but no decision was reached. The model captures only that a PO is raised against a Vendor and has a status constraint; it does not and cannot capture post-suspension fulfillment behavior. This is a known open item and should be addressed once policy is decided by the sourcing steering group.

source_references.excerpt: If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list -- what happens to the purchase orders already in flight?... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Vendor-to-region cardinality: The transcript confirms that a vendor can operate in multiple regions (line 167: 'Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region'), which implies a many-to-many relationship at the logical level. However, the model captures this as a ternary fact 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact,' which constrains the pairing. For clarity: does every Vendor-Region pair that exists in the system ALWAYS have an associated Contact, or can a Vendor be 'registered' to operate in a Region without yet having a contact assigned? The transcript suggests the latter is not possible (line 163 shows the system enforces the uniqueness of the primary contact per vendor-region), but the optional participation logic is not explicitly stated.

source_references.excerpt: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region... Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Spend tier assignment logic: The transcript states 'Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them' (line 285), which clearly establishes that SpendTier is mandatory with Bronze as default. However, it does not explain the business rule for determining non-Bronze tiers. Who decides when a vendor is promoted to Silver or Gold? Is there a documented criteria (e.g., annual spend threshold), or is it subjective? The model captures the constraint but not the decision logic.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

ambiguities.description: Conflict between procurement and compliance enforcement: Dana (Procurement Lead) states 'my team has been treating the W-9 as the gate' for when a vendor can be used (line 89), but Raj (Compliance Officer) corrects this: 'the system does enforce it -- you cannot move a vendor to active without a completed review' (line 91). Mei corroborates that vendors are being used despite this rule, suggesting a disconnect between business process and system enforcement. The model captures the rule as it should be (Active status requires a current signed-off review), but the transcript reveals actual practice differs. This is noted as a known discrepancy but is NOT modeled as an alternative rule, per the instruction to capture rules as they are, not as they should be. However, the model should reflect the actual system enforcement (line 91), not the workaround.

source_references.excerpt: my team has been treating the W-9 as the gate... What happens is procurement thinks the vendor is ready, tells the buyer it's ready, the buyer tries to raise the PO, it fails, and then it comes to me.

ambiguities.description: Terminology ambiguity: 'Tier' is overloaded. Dana uses 'tier' to mean SpendTier (Bronze, Silver, Gold), while Raj uses 'tier' to mean RiskTier (Low, Medium, High). The facilitator explicitly notes this conflict (line 137: 'half the room hears big spender and the other half hears dangerous'). While the model correctly distinguishes these as two independent attributes, the ambiguous use of the single term 'tier' in the business remains a communication risk. The term should be disambiguated in process documentation as 'spend tier' and 'risk tier,' but this is an organizational/linguistic issue rather than a data modeling issue.

source_references.excerpt: you said tier earlier... Dana: I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with... Raj: And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high... We've asked people to say spend tier and risk tier. Nobody does.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID uniqueness assumption vs. reality: The transcript confirms that TaxId is NOT a unique identifier (line 45: 'We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident'). The model correctly makes VendorNumber the identifier and allows multiple vendors to share a TaxId. However, the transcript also notes an ongoing duplicate-resolution project (line 47: 'The duplicates are a real problem. There's a cleanup project that's been on the roadmap for two years'), which suggests the current data state may violate intended business logic. The model captures the current rules correctly, but stakeholders should be aware that historical data contains duplicates that do not conform to the intended constraint that TaxId should ideally identify a unique entity.

source_references.excerpt: And could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead?... You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID... Noted, but out of scope for today. Tax ID isn't an identifier, vendor number is.
